item.title: The Science Talk Signs the EU Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content
item.description:
We signed the European Commission’s Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content, under Section 2, as a deployer of generative AI systems. That puts The Science Talk in the same signatory pool as Bulgari, Getty Images, Lenovo, and Lufthansa. Section 1 of the framework counts Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Mistral among its signatories.

Why this, why now

The AI Act’s transparency obligations become legally binding on 2 August 2026. These are the rules that require AI-generated and AI-modified content to be marked and disclosed. The Commission approved the Code of Practice as the sanctioned route to compliance. Independent experts drafted it. The Commission and the AI Board found it sufficient. It gives signatories “a streamlined, predictable and legally certain pathway,” regardless of which national authority ends up supervising them.

item.title: Regulation as a Feature: The Case for AI Transparency
item.description:
Every conversation I have about the EU AI Act’s transparency rules starts from the same assumption: this is a cost to be minimised. Add the disclosure, tick the box, move on. I think that framing gets the opportunity backwards — AI transparency, done properly, is a genuine competitive advantage for a small AI-using team competing against operators who treat it as an afterthought.

The obligation, stated plainly

Article 50 of the AI Act requires providers of certain AI systems to make clear that people are interacting with AI, and requires marking of AI-generated or manipulated content — including deepfakes and AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest. These duties apply from 2 August 2026, and — following the 2026 Digital Omnibus — generative AI systems already on the market before that date have a transitional period extended to 2 December 2026 to comply with the content-marking requirement specifically.

item.title: EU AI Act Article 50 Is Now in Force: What Changed on 2 August 2026
item.description: As of 2 August 2026, Article 50 of the EU AI Act has stopped being “the thing everyone’s been meaning to prepare for” and is an enforceable transparency obligation. If you publish AI-generated or AI-manipulated content professionally — text, video, audio, social posts — this is the date the disclosure duty starts to bite. Here’s what that means in practice, and what it doesn’t.

item.title: The EU AI Act: Everything Digital Creators Need to Know
item.description: Most digital creators I talk to think the EU AI Act means one thing: slap an “AI-generated” tag on your video and move on. It doesn’t. Article 50 is the part with a hard deadline — 2 August 2026 — so it gets all the attention. But it’s one article inside a bigger framework, and creators who only prepare for the label are missing the parts that actually restrict how they can build and use AI tools.

item.title: How to add AI disclosures that comply with the EU AI Act
item.description: The EU AI Act’s transparency obligations under Article 50 apply from 2 August 2026 — and if you publish AI-generated content professionally, you have specific disclosure duties that go well beyond adding a footnote to your terms and conditions. The European Commission has published draft guidelines explaining exactly what those disclosures must look like, where they must appear, and what will not meet the standard. This guide translates those requirements into practical placement guidance for content creators, freelancers, and science communicators.
